title: Artery of Percheron infarction: a case report
case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man was found unconscious at home with open doors and windows and brought to the emergency department. On arrival he developed ventricular fibrillation; cardiopulmonary resuscitation restored sinus rhythm after two defibrillations and cardiopulmonary bypass was used for rewarming, with total ventricular fibrillation duration under 2 minutes. His history included heavy alcohol use and 20 cigarettes per day; no medication data were available.

On examination his temperature was 24.5 °C, blood pressure 145/70 mmHg, heart rate 35 bpm, and respiratory rate 8–10 /min. He was unconscious (RLS-85 score 4) and had slight anisocoria (right pupil larger than left). Heart and lung auscultation were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed moderate electrolyte disturbances and elevated liver enzymes; drug and alcohol screens were negative.

Noncontrast head CT on admission was interpreted as normal, with no hemorrhage or acute infarction. In the ICU he was sedated and ventilated; his course was complicated by pneumothorax after CPR, pneumonia, bilateral pleural effusions, intestinal paralysis, acute pancreatitis, and ascites. Sedation was discontinued two weeks after admission. He opened his eyes to voice but was nonverbal; he withdrew his arms, moved his left foot, and grimaced to pain. He again had slight anisocoria (left pupil now larger) but symmetric pupillary reflexes. EEG showed irregular theta/delta activity without epileptiform discharges.

On hospital day 24, repeat head CT revealed bilateral ischemia in the medial thalami and a smaller ischemic area in the left pons.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Top-of-the-basilar syndrome was considered but excluded because there were no infarcts in the superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral artery territories — “Top of the basilar syndrome can present with bilateral thalamic infarcts but there are usually also infarcts present within the vascular territories of the superior cerebellar artery and posterior cerebral artery.”  
2. Deep cerebral venous thrombosis was considered but imaging did not show basal ganglia involvement or signs of venous occlusion — “Deep cerebral venous thrombosis can in rare instances result in bilateral symmetric involvement of the thalamus and basal ganglia.”  
3. Wernicke’s encephalopathy was considered but characteristic MRI findings in the tectal plate, periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies, and dorsal medulla were absent — “Wernicke’s encephalopathy can also be a differential diagnosis of bilateral thalamic lesions, in which T2-weighted MRI findings include symmetric hyperintensity in the medial thalami but also in the tectal plate, periaqueductal gray, mamillary bodies, and dorsal medulla.”  
4. Neoplasm, infection, Wilson’s disease, and osmotic myelinolysis were listed as potential causes of bilateral thalamic lesions but lacked supportive clinical or imaging features — “Differential diagnoses also include neoplasms, infections, Wilson’s disease, and osmotic myelinolysis.”
